design_note: The prior labs distinguish missing telemetry from missing effects and enforce recording policy. These durations add a debugging trap: child spans are already included in their parent's elapsed time. The reader reconstructs the timeline instead of summing overlapping measurements into a false latency.

source.title: Traces
source.concept: Spans record units of work with start/end times and parent identifiers. Child spans represent sub-operations, so nested span durations are not disjoint pieces of elapsed time.
source.scope: All intervals and durations are constructed. One synchronous run contains sequential model and tool spans inside its investigation span; no general timing relationship for all traces is implied.

lesson.anchor: Debugging a bad trajectory: a worked example
lesson.title: Nested spans are not extra seconds
lesson.intro: This constructed trace has a run from 0-12 s, investigation from 2-10 s, model call from 2-7 s, and tool read from 7-10 s. Model and tool are children of investigation.

data.rule: Parent intervals contain their children; summing all four bars counts time repeatedly.

read: The run's wall-clock duration is 12 seconds.
The 5-second model call and 3-second tool read occupy the 8-second investigation.
Four seconds of the run lie outside investigation: 0-2 s and 10-12 s.
lesson.question: Does adding the four durations mean the customer waited 28 seconds?
lesson.answer: No. The sum counts nested work repeatedly. The customer-visible run spans 12 seconds; the investigation already contains its two children. Use actual start/end relationships to calculate elapsed time and distinguish parent duration from time spent outside child operations.
lesson.takeaway: Read span containment before adding durations.
lesson.assumption: Toy trace, not measured performance; one clock and synchronous nesting. No omitted wait or concurrent branch exists within the shown investigation.
